> Anamnestic anti-Jkᵃ/Jkᵇ, anti-E/c, anti-Fyᵃ, anti-K (missed because titre was undetectable pretransfusion).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Prevention: obtain transfusion/pregnancy history, keep antibody records (national databases), use sensitive screening (homozygous cells), and give antigen-negative blood for any historical antibody even if now undetectable.

## Simplified explanation

Delayed reactions happen when a patient's old antibody (often Kidd, Rh, Duffy or Kell) was too weak to detect but bounces back after transfusion.

body: State three (3) antigens that exhibit dosage.
answer:
Any three: **Rh** (C, c, E, e), **Kidd** (Jkᵃ, Jkᵇ), **Duffy** (Fyᵃ, Fyᵇ), **MNS** (M, N, S, s).

> [!answer]
> Kidd (Jkᵃ), Duffy (Fyᵃ), Rh (c/E) (also M, N, S, s).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Dosage**: antibodies react more strongly with cells **homozygous** for the antigen (double dose, e.g. Jk(a+b−)) than heterozygous cells (Jk(a+b+)). Screening cells should be homozygous for these antigens so weak antibodies are not missed.

## Simplified explanation

Kidd, Duffy, Rh and MNS antigens show dosage: double-dose cells react more strongly.

body: State one disadvantage of using polyethylene glycol (PEG) as an enhancement medium during antibody screening procedures.
answer:
Any one: PEG **enhances warm autoantibodies** and clinically insignificant antibodies (unwanted positives); tests **cannot be centrifuged/read before washing** (PEG causes non-specific aggregation, so no immediate-spin or 37 °C reading); not suitable for some automated/column systems; may give false positives with some plasma proteins.

> [!answer]
> It increases detection of autoantibodies/insignificant antibodies (and cannot be read before the AHG phase).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

PEG is a water-soluble polymer that removes water, concentrating antibody around cells; it is highly sensitive for weak IgG alloantibodies, but the gain comes with more unwanted reactivity.

## Simplified explanation

PEG is very sensitive, so it also picks up autoantibodies and harmless antibodies.

body: In not more than two sentences, differentiate between fresh frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate.
answer:
**Fresh frozen plasma** is plasma separated from whole blood and frozen (≤ −18 °C to −25 °C) within ~8 hours of collection; it contains **all coagulation factors** (including labile V and VIII) and other plasma proteins. **Cryoprecipitate** is the **cold-insoluble precipitate** formed when FFP is thawed slowly at 1–6 °C, re-suspended in a small volume of plasma and refrozen; it is concentrated in **fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII and fibronectin**.

> [!answer]
> FFP = whole plasma with all factors; cryo = cold precipitate from thawed FFP rich in fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, FXIII.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Typical doses: FFP 12–15 ml/kg for multiple factor deficiency (DIC, massive transfusion, liver disease); cryoprecipitate pools (~10 units adult) for fibrinogen <1.5 g/L. Cryo-poor plasma is used in TTP plasma exchange.

## Simplified explanation

FFP is frozen plasma with every clotting factor; cryo is the cold sludge from thawed FFP that is rich in fibrinogen and factor VIII.

body: State two (2) uses of cryoprecipitate.
answer:
Any two:

- **Hypofibrinogenaemia** (fibrinogen <1–1.5 g/L) in **DIC**, massive transfusion, obstetric haemorrhage, liver disease.
- **Congenital fibrinogen deficiency/dysfibrinogenaemia**.
- **Factor XIII deficiency**.
- **von Willebrand disease** or **haemophilia A** when concentrates are unavailable.
- Uraemic bleeding; preparation of fibrin glue.

> [!answer]
> Fibrinogen replacement (DIC, massive haemorrhage) and vWD/haemophilia A or FXIII deficiency when concentrates are unavailable.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Each unit of cryoprecipitate contains ≥140 mg fibrinogen (UK) / ≥150 mg (AABB) and ≥70–80 IU FVIII. Fibrinogen concentrate is increasingly used instead.

## Simplified explanation

Cryo is mainly given to replace fibrinogen in heavy bleeding or DIC, and for vWD/haemophilia A or FXIII deficiency if factor concentrates aren't available.

body: State the difference between "STAT" and "ASAP" if indicated on a laboratory requisition.
answer:
**STAT** (from Latin *statim*, 'immediately') means the request is an **emergency/life-threatening priority** and must be processed **immediately**, ahead of all other work, with results phoned/reported within the shortest turnaround (e.g. <1 h). **ASAP** ('as soon as possible') is **urgent but not an emergency**: processed promptly, after STAT requests but before routine work.

> [!answer]
> STAT = immediate, highest priority (emergency); ASAP = urgent, next priority after STAT.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Laboratories define priority categories and target turnaround times (STAT, urgent/ASAP, routine) in their service level agreements; overuse of STAT requests degrades turnaround for genuine emergencies.

## Simplified explanation

STAT means do it right now (emergency). ASAP means do it soon, but after STAT work.

body: State the main difference (at the molecular level) between the C and c Rh antigens.
answer:
C and c are antithetical antigens on the **RhCE protein** that differ by **four amino acids** (positions 16, 60, 68 and 103: Cys16Trp, Ile60Leu, Ser68Asn, **Ser103Pro**); the extracellular **Ser103 (C) / Pro103 (c)** substitution determines C versus c antigenicity.

> [!answer]
> Four amino acid differences on RhCE; Ser103 = C, Pro103 = c.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

RHCE alleles: Ce, cE, ce, CE. E/e differ by a single amino acid (**Pro226Ala**: E = Pro226, e = Ala226). RhD differs from RhCE by 32–35 amino acids.

## Simplified explanation

C and c differ by four amino acids in the RhCE protein, the key one being serine (C) vs proline (c) at position 103.

body: State the main difference between the RHD and RHCE gene products with regards to the Rh blood group system.
answer:
The **RHD** gene encodes the **RhD protein**, which carries the **D antigen**; the **RHCE** gene encodes the **RhCE protein**, which carries the **C/c and E/e antigens**. The two highly homologous proteins differ by **32–35 amino acids**; D-negative people (in Europeans) usually lack RHD entirely, whereas everyone has an RHCE.

> [!answer]
> RHD → RhD (D antigen); RHCE → RhCE (C/c, E/e), differing by ~32–35 amino acids.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

RHD and RHCE lie close together on chromosome 1p36, in opposite orientation, flanked by Rhesus boxes (deletion of RHD by unequal crossing over). In Africans, D-negativity can also result from the RHDψ pseudogene or RHD-CE-D hybrids.

## Simplified explanation

One gene makes the protein with D; the other makes the protein with C/c and E/e. They differ by about 35 amino acids.

body: In not more than two sentences, explain 'high frequency' antigen.
answer:
A high-frequency (high-prevalence/public) antigen is a red cell antigen present in **more than 99% of the population** (e.g. k, Kpᵇ, Lubᵇ, Vel, U, Jsᵇ in most populations). People who lack it are rare, so if they form the antibody, **compatible (antigen-negative) blood is very difficult to find** and every panel cell reacts.

> [!answer]
> An antigen found in >99% of people; its antibody reacts with almost all donor cells.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Low-frequency (private) antigens occur in <1% (e.g. Kpᵃ, Jsᵃ in Europeans, Wrᵃ). For antibodies to high-frequency antigens, rare donor registries, frozen rare units and family (sibling) testing are used.

## Simplified explanation

It's an antigen almost everyone has, so a patient who lacks it and makes the antibody is very hard to find blood for.

body: State the reason why blood for exchange transfusion must be irradiated to kill lymphocytes.
answer:
To prevent **transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GvHD)**: viable donor T lymphocytes could engraft in the neonate, whose immune system is immature (especially after intrauterine transfusion), and attack the recipient's tissues (skin, liver, gut, marrow), which is usually fatal.

> [!answer]
> Inactivate donor T cells to prevent TA-GvHD in the immunologically immature neonate.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Irradiation (25 Gy minimum) blocks lymphocyte proliferation; irradiated red cells should be used within 24 h of irradiation for exchange transfusion (K⁺ leak) and expire 14 days after irradiation otherwise.

## Simplified explanation

Radiation kills donor white cells so they can't attack the baby (graft-versus-host disease).

body: What volume of packed red cells can be neutralised by 150 µg of Rh anti-D immune globulin?
answer:
A **300 µg** dose neutralises **15 ml of D-positive packed red cells** (≈30 ml fetal whole blood), i.e. ~20 µg per ml of red cells. Therefore **150 µg neutralises ~7.5 ml of packed red cells** (~15 ml whole blood).

> [!answer]
> About 7.5 ml packed red cells (15 ml whole blood).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

AABB convention: 300 µg (1500 IU) per 15 ml RBC / 30 ml whole blood. UK (BSH) convention uses 125 IU (25 µg) per ml of fetal red cells, which would give 6 ml for 150 µg; check the convention used in your course.

## Simplified explanation

300 µg covers 15 ml of red cells, so half that dose covers half: 7.5 ml.

body: State two (2) main differences between immune antibody and non-immune antibody.
answer:
Any two:

| Immune antibody | Non-immune (naturally occurring) antibody |
|---|---|
| Formed after **red cell stimulation** (transfusion, pregnancy) | Formed **without known red cell exposure** (environmental antigens) |
| Mainly **IgG** | Mainly **IgM** |
| Reacts best at **37 °C** (IAT) | Reacts best at **room temperature/4 °C** (saline agglutinins) |
| Crosses the placenta → HDFN | Does not cross the placenta |
| Usually clinically significant (e.g. anti-D, -K, -Jkᵃ) | Often insignificant (except anti-A, -B) |

> [!answer]
> Immune = red-cell-stimulated, IgG, warm, crosses placenta; non-immune = no stimulus, IgM, cold, does not cross placenta.
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Naturally occurring antibodies (anti-A, -B, -M, -N, -P1, -Leᵃ, -Leᵇ, -I) arise from exposure to similar carbohydrate antigens on bacteria, food and pollen. ABO antibodies are the important exception: IgM, natural, yet highly haemolytic.

## Simplified explanation

Immune antibodies come after exposure to foreign red cells and are warm IgG; natural ones appear on their own and are cold IgM.

body: State two applications of indirect antiglobulin test.
answer:
Any two: **antibody screening** and **identification**; **crossmatching** (AHG crossmatch); **weak D testing**; red cell **phenotyping** with IgG antisera (e.g. Duffy, Kidd); **antibody titration** (e.g. anti-D in pregnancy).

> [!answer]
> e.g. antibody screening/identification and crossmatching (also weak D testing, titration).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

IAT: in-vitro sensitisation of red cells by antibody at 37 °C, washing to remove unbound globulin, then AHG reagent to bridge IgG-coated cells.

## Simplified explanation

The IAT is used to screen for and identify antibodies, crossmatch blood and test for weak D.

body: In not more than two sentences explain 'McLeod phenotype'.
answer:
The McLeod phenotype is a rare **X-linked** condition in which red cells **lack the Kx antigen** (XK gene defect), resulting in **markedly weakened Kell antigens**. It is associated with **acanthocytosis**, compensated haemolysis, raised CK and late-onset neuromuscular disease (McLeod syndrome), and sometimes **X-linked chronic granulomatous disease**.

> [!answer]
> X-linked absence of Kx with weak Kell antigens and acanthocytes (± CGD).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Kx (XK protein) is linked to the Kell glycoprotein by a disulphide bond. McLeod males transfused may make anti-Kx + anti-Km and need McLeod blood (or Kx−) units.

## Simplified explanation

McLeod people (usually men) lack Kx, so Kell antigens are weak and red cells are spiky (acanthocytes).

body: You are supposed to draw blood from a prospective donor. By your calculation, you can draw a maximum of 300 ml whole blood. The blood bag contains 63 ml anticoagulant. How much of the anticoagulant should be expelled from the blood bag to reflect the volume of whole blood to be collected?
answer:
Anticoagulant needed = 63 ml × 300 ÷ 450 = **42 ml**.

Anticoagulant to expel = 63 − 42 = **21 ml**.

> [!answer]
> Expel 21 ml (leave 42 ml).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Standard bags hold 63 ml CPD/CPDA-1 for 450 ml (or 70 ml for 500 ml). For low-volume collections, excess anticoagulant is expressed into a satellite bag and sealed off before collection to keep the 1:7 ratio and avoid citrate excess (dilution, red cell shrinkage).

## Simplified explanation

300 ml needs two thirds of the 63 ml, i.e. 42 ml, so squeeze out 21 ml.

body: State five (5) parasites that can be transmitted through blood transfusion.
answer:
Any five: ***Plasmodium* spp.** (malaria), ***Trypanosoma cruzi*** (Chagas disease), ***Babesia microti***, ***Leishmania* spp.**, ***Toxoplasma gondii***, ***Trypanosoma brucei***, microfilariae (***Wuchereria bancrofti***, ***Loa loa***, *Brugia*).

> [!answer]
> Plasmodium, Trypanosoma cruzi, Babesia, Leishmania, Toxoplasma (also T. brucei, microfilariae).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Malaria is the commonest transfusion-transmitted parasitic infection in endemic areas such as Ghana; parasites survive in stored red cells. Prevention: donor questioning/deferral, malaria testing in some settings, pathogen reduction, and prophylaxis for vulnerable recipients.

## Simplified explanation

Malaria parasites, trypanosomes, Babesia, Leishmania and Toxoplasma can be passed on by transfusion.

body: State three (3) bacterial infections that can be transmitted by blood transfusion.
answer:
Any three: **syphilis** (*Treponema pallidum*), **brucellosis**, ***Yersinia enterocolitica*** sepsis (stored red cells), **staphylococcal/streptococcal** sepsis (skin contaminants in platelets, e.g. *S. epidermidis*, *S. aureus*), ***Serratia*/*Pseudomonas*** contamination, **rickettsial** infections, **Lyme disease** (*Borrelia*) rarely.

> [!answer]
> Syphilis, Yersinia enterocolitica sepsis, staphylococcal sepsis (also brucellosis, Serratia, Pseudomonas).
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Bacterial contamination arises from donor skin (prevented by skin disinfection and diversion of the first 20–30 ml), asymptomatic donor bacteraemia, or processing. Platelets (stored at 22 °C) carry the highest risk; *Yersinia* grows in refrigerated red cells.

## Simplified explanation

Syphilis, Yersinia and skin bacteria like Staphylococcus can get into blood units.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Platelet refractoriness may be due to all the following ...

A. ABO incompatibility
B. MHC class II incompatibility
C. Rh D antigen incompatibility
D. Hypersplenism
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. ABO incompatibility | **T** | ABO-incompatible platelets give lower increments. |
| B. MHC class II incompatibility | **F** | Platelets express HLA class I, not class II. |
| C. Rh D antigen incompatibility | **F** | Platelets do not carry RhD. |
| D. Hypersplenism | **T** | Splenic sequestration is a non-immune cause. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Platelet refractoriness**: poor count increments after repeated transfusions. **Immune** causes: **HLA class I** antibodies (commonest), HPA antibodies, ABO incompatibility. **Non-immune**: fever, sepsis, DIC, **splenomegaly/hypersplenism**, drugs (amphotericin, vancomycin), bleeding, HSCT.

## Simplified explanation

ABO mismatch and a big spleen can stop platelet transfusions working; HLA class II and RhD aren't on platelets.
hint: Platelets carry HLA class I and ABO.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The differences between cryoprecipitate and cryopoor plasma include all the following ...

A. Cryoprecipitate contains FVIII which is absent in cryopoor plasma
B. Cryopoor plasma contains vWF which is absent in cryoprecipitate
C. Cryopoor plasma is the part of frozen plasma that remains solid when thawed at 4°C whereas the cryoprecipitate is the liquid component of frozen plasma thawed at 4°C
D. Cryoprecipitate is deficient in cryoglobulin which is present in cryopoor plasma
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Cryoprecipitate contains FVIII which is absent in cryopoor plasma | **T** | FVIII is concentrated in cryo; cryo-poor plasma is depleted of it. |
| B. Cryopoor plasma contains vWF which is absent in cryoprecipitate | **F** | vWF (especially large multimers) is concentrated in **cryoprecipitate**. |
| C. Cryopoor plasma is the part of frozen plasma that remains solid when thawed at 4°C whereas the cryoprecipitate is the liquid component of frozen plasma thawed at 4°C | **F** | Reversed: cryoprecipitate is the cold-insoluble (solid) part; cryo-poor plasma is the supernatant. |
| D. Cryoprecipitate is deficient in cryoglobulin which is present in cryopoor plasma | **F** | Cold-insoluble proteins precipitate into cryo. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Thawing FFP at 1–6 °C leaves a **cold-insoluble precipitate** (cryoprecipitate: fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF, FXIII, fibronectin) and a supernatant (**cryo-poor/cryosupernatant plasma**), depleted of these but with other factors; used in TTP plasma exchange (low in large vWF multimers).

## Simplified explanation

Cryo is the solid sludge rich in FVIII, vWF and fibrinogen; cryo-poor plasma is what's left and lacks them.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The hepatitis B profile of a client was as follows: HBsAg (−); HBeAg (−); anti-HBs (+); anti-HBe (+); anti-HBc total (+). These findings are suggestive of ...

A. The client is in the window period
B. The client is in acute phase of the infection
C. The client is in the chronic phase of infection
D. The client is in the recovery period and immunized
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. The client is in the window period | **F** | Window period: HBsAg−, anti-HBs−, anti-HBc IgM+. |
| B. The client is in acute phase of the infection | **F** | Acute: HBsAg+, anti-HBc IgM+. |
| C. The client is in the chronic phase of infection | **F** | Chronic: HBsAg+ >6 months. |
| D. The client is in the recovery period and immunized | **T** | Resolved infection with natural immunity. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Resolved HBV infection**: HBsAg−, **anti-HBs+**, **anti-HBc+** (IgG), anti-HBe+. **Vaccinated**: anti-HBs+ only. **Acute**: HBsAg+, HBeAg+, anti-HBc IgM+. **Window**: only anti-HBc IgM+. **Chronic**: HBsAg+ >6 months, anti-HBc IgG+.

## Simplified explanation

Having anti-HBs and anti-HBc without HBsAg means past infection that has cleared, with immunity.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following viruses are associated with cellular blood components ...

A. HTLV-1
B. HIV-1
C. Parvovirus
D. Hepatitis C
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. HTLV-1 | **T** | Strictly cell-associated (lymphocytes). |
| B. HIV-1 | **T** | Infects CD4⁺ cells (also free in plasma). |
| C. Parvovirus | **F** | Plasma-borne (heat-resistant, transmitted by plasma products). |
| D. Hepatitis C | **F** | Plasma-borne. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Cell-associated** viruses (reduced by leucodepletion): HTLV-I/II, **CMV**, EBV, HHV-8, HIV (cellular and free). **Plasma-borne**: HBV, HCV, HIV, parvovirus B19, HAV, West Nile.

## Simplified explanation

HTLV-1 and HIV-1 live in white cells; parvovirus and hepatitis C travel in plasma.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In the serological tests used to stage hepatitis B virus infection, the following indicates highly infectious stage ...

A. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (+), anti-HBc IgG (+) serum
B. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgG (+) serum
C. HBsAg (−), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgM (+) serum
D. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgM (+) serum
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (+), anti-HBc IgG (+) serum | **T** | HBeAg positivity indicates high viral replication. |
| B. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgG (+) serum | **F** | Lower infectivity (HBeAg-negative), unless an HBeAg-negative mutant. |
| C. HBsAg (−), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgM (+) serum | **F** | Window period: lower infectivity. |
| D. HBsAg (+), HBeAg (−), anti-HBc IgM (+) serum | **F** | Acute infection, but HBeAg negative indicates lower replication. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**HBeAg** is a marker of active viral replication and high infectivity (high HBV DNA). Seroconversion to anti-HBe usually indicates lower replication (except precore mutants). HBV DNA quantification is the definitive measure.

## Simplified explanation

HBeAg positivity (with HBsAg) means the virus is multiplying a lot and is highly infectious.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following cells have CD4 receptors and may serve as reservoirs for HIV ...

A. Monocytes
B. Macrophages
C. Neutrophils
D. T4 lymphocytes
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Monocytes | **T** | Express CD4 and CCR5. |
| B. Macrophages | **T** | Major tissue reservoir. |
| C. Neutrophils | **F** | Do not express CD4 significantly. |
| D. T4 lymphocytes | **T** | CD4⁺ helper T cells, the main target and latent reservoir. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

HIV gp120 binds **CD4** plus co-receptor **CCR5** (macrophage-tropic) or **CXCR4** (T-tropic). Reservoirs: resting memory CD4⁺ T cells, monocytes/macrophages, microglia, dendritic cells.

## Simplified explanation

HIV hides in CD4 T cells, monocytes and macrophages, not neutrophils.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Cryoprecipitate contains ...

A. Factor VII
B. Factor XIII
C. Factor I
D. von Willebrand factor
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Factor VII | **F** | Remains in cryo-poor plasma. |
| B. Factor XIII | **T** | Concentrated in cryo. |
| C. Factor I | **T** | Fibrinogen is the main content. |
| D. von Willebrand factor | **T** | Concentrated in cryo. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C T, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cryoprecipitate: **fibrinogen (factor I)**, **FVIII**, **vWF**, **FXIII**, fibronectin. It lacks significant amounts of factors II, V, VII, IX, X, XI.

## Simplified explanation

Cryo contains fibrinogen, FVIII, vWF and FXIII, not factor VII.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following statements are all true about cryoprecipitate

A. It's a rich source of vitamin K dependent coagulation factors
B. It could be used to treat von Willebrands disease
C. It must be thawed at 4°C to preserve factor activity
D. It may be used to treat haemophilia A
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. It's a rich source of vitamin K dependent coagulation factors | **F** | Vitamin K-dependent factors (II, VII, IX, X) are not concentrated in cryo; use PCC/FFP. |
| B. It could be used to treat von Willebrands disease | **T** | When vWF concentrate is unavailable. |
| C. It must be thawed at 4°C to preserve factor activity | **F** | For use it is thawed at **30–37 °C** (it is prepared by slow thawing of FFP at 1–6 °C). |
| D. It may be used to treat haemophilia A | **T** | Contains FVIII (when concentrate unavailable). |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Cryoprecipitate is stored at ≤ −18 °C and thawed at 30–37 °C before use (then kept at room temperature, used within 4–6 h). Indications: hypofibrinogenaemia, and vWD/haemophilia A/FXIII deficiency only if specific concentrates are unavailable.

## Simplified explanation

Cryo can treat vWD and haemophilia A; it isn't a source of vitamin K factors and is warmed (not kept at 4 °C) before use.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The following statements are all true about irradiation of red blood cells ...

A. It inactivates residual lymphocytes
B. It helps to prevent graft-versus-leukaemia effect
C. It increases the chances of a graft-versus-host disease
D. It is indicated for blood meant for neonatal transfusion
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. It inactivates residual lymphocytes | **T** | Prevents donor T-cell proliferation. |
| B. It helps to prevent graft-versus-leukaemia effect | **F** | GvL is a desired effect in HSCT; not the aim of irradiation. |
| C. It increases the chances of a graft-versus-host disease | **F** | It **prevents** TA-GvHD. |
| D. It is indicated for blood meant for neonatal transfusion | **T** | Per the key; specifically for IUT, exchange transfusion and preterm/immunodeficient neonates. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Irradiation (≥25 Gy) inactivates T lymphocytes to prevent **TA-GvHD**. Indications: IUT and neonatal exchange (and transfusion after IUT), congenital T-cell immunodeficiency, HSCT, Hodgkin lymphoma, purine analogues, HLA-selected/related-donor components. Irradiated red cells have shortened shelf life (K⁺ leak).

## Simplified explanation

Irradiation kills donor lymphocytes to stop TA-GvHD and is used for vulnerable newborns.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

MHC class II antigens may be important in the transfusion of all the following blood products as they may cause immunization ...

A. Packed red blood cells
B. Granulocytes
C. Platelet concentrate
D. B-lymphocytes
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Packed red blood cells | **F** | Red cells lack HLA class II (residual leucocytes aside). |
| B. Granulocytes | **T** | Granulocyte concentrates contain HLA class II-bearing cells. |
| C. Platelet concentrate | **F** | Platelets carry class I only. |
| D. B-lymphocytes | **T** | B cells express HLA class II. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**HLA class II** (DR, DQ, DP) is expressed on B cells, monocytes/macrophages, dendritic cells and activated T cells. Leucocytes in components (especially granulocyte concentrates) can cause HLA alloimmunisation; leucodepletion reduces this.

## Simplified explanation

Class II antigens are on white cells like B lymphocytes and in granulocyte products, not on red cells or platelets.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Patient #0023 experienced an acute transfusion reaction. Examination of his first voided urine gave: bilirubin (4+), raised urobilinogen, RBC casts, haemoglobinuria. These findings are consistent with ...

A. Immune-mediated RBC destruction
B. Non-immune mediated RBC destruction
C. Intravascular haemolysis
D. Extravascular haemolysis
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Immune-mediated RBC destruction | **T** | Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction is antibody (usually ABO) mediated. |
| B. Non-immune mediated RBC destruction | **F** | The setting (acute transfusion reaction) points to an immune cause. |
| C. Intravascular haemolysis | **T** | Haemoglobinuria indicates intravascular lysis. |
| D. Extravascular haemolysis | **F** | Haemoglobinuria is a feature of intravascular haemolysis. |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

An **acute haemolytic transfusion reaction** (usually ABO incompatibility) involves complement-fixing IgM/IgG antibodies that lyse donor cells **intravascularly**: haemoglobinaemia, **haemoglobinuria**, raised bilirubin/LDH, low haptoglobin, positive DAT, possible DIC and acute kidney injury.

## Simplified explanation

Haemoglobin in the urine during a transfusion reaction means immune destruction of red cells inside the vessels.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Mr Ocansey had a transfusion 3 days ago. He returned to the laboratory with jaundice, loss of energy and pallor. His laboratory findings were: raised serum bilirubin, normal serum haptoglobin, positive DAT, raised urobilinogen, absent urine casts, absent urine haemoglobin, and a 2 g/dl drop in haemoglobin. These laboratory findings are consistent with ...

A. Intravascular RBC destruction
B. Extravascular haemolytic transfusion reaction
C. Graft-versus-host reaction
D. Nonimmune mediated transfusion reaction
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Intravascular RBC destruction | **F** | No haemoglobinuria, normal haptoglobin. |
| B. Extravascular haemolytic transfusion reaction | **T** | Delayed, extravascular, DAT-positive haemolysis. |
| C. Graft-versus-host reaction | **F** | TA-GvHD presents with fever, rash, diarrhoea, pancytopenia ~1–2 weeks later. |
| D. Nonimmune mediated transfusion reaction | **F** | Positive DAT indicates immune destruction. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B T, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Delayed haemolytic transfusion reaction** (3–14 days): anamnestic IgG alloantibody (e.g. Kidd, Rh) coats transfused cells, which are removed **extravascularly**: falling Hb, jaundice, raised bilirubin and urobilinogen, **positive DAT**, new antibody in serum, spherocytes; haemoglobinuria is absent.

## Simplified explanation

Jaundice and a falling Hb days after transfusion, with a positive DAT but no haemoglobin in urine, is a delayed extravascular reaction.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The antibody titration results of patients #1 and #2 are recorded below.

| | 1:2 | 1:4 | 1:8 | 1:16 | 1:32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| #1 | 2+ | 2+ | 1+ | 1+ | 0 |
| #2 | 3+ | 3+ | 2+ | 2+ | 1+ |

A. The antibody titre of patient #1 is 0.0625
B. The antibody titre of patient #2 is 32
C. The antibody titre of patient #1 is 32
D. The antibody titre of patient #2 cannot be determined from data
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. The antibody titre of patient #1 is 0.0625 | **F** | Titre is the **reciprocal** of the highest dilution giving 1+: **16**. |
| B. The antibody titre of patient #2 is 32 | **F** | Still reacting at 1:32, so the end-point has not been reached (≥32). |
| C. The antibody titre of patient #1 is 32 | **F** | 1:32 is negative; titre = 16. |
| D. The antibody titre of patient #2 cannot be determined from data | **T** | Further dilutions are needed. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Titre** = reciprocal of the highest dilution showing macroscopic (1+) agglutination. If the last dilution tested is still positive, the titre is reported as '≥ that value' and more dilutions are needed. A titre score (weighting reaction strengths) can also be calculated. In pregnancy, a change of ≥2 dilutions (fourfold) is significant.

## Simplified explanation

Patient 1's last positive is 1:16, so titre 16. Patient 2 is still positive at 1:32, so the end point is unknown.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

Coombs control cells ...

A. Are group O Rh D positive IgG coated cells
B. Can be prepared by adding 8 drops of group O Rh D negative cells to 6 drops of 6% bovine albumin
C. Can be prepared by adding one drop of whole blood to one drop of slide-tube reagent Rh D
D. Is used to confirm positive DAT testing
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Are group O Rh D positive IgG coated cells | **T** | O D+ cells sensitised with anti-D (IgG). |
| B. Can be prepared by adding 8 drops of group O Rh D negative cells to 6 drops of 6% bovine albumin | **F** | They require D+ cells sensitised with IgG anti-D, not albumin. |
| C. Can be prepared by adding one drop of whole blood to one drop of slide-tube reagent Rh D | **F** | They are made by incubating washed O D+ cells with diluted IgG anti-D at 37 °C and washing. |
| D. Is used to confirm positive DAT testing | **F** | They confirm **negative** AHG tests (check that AHG was active). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

**Check cells (Coombs control cells)**: group O RhD-positive red cells sensitised with IgG anti-D. Added to every **negative** IAT/DAT tube after reading; agglutination confirms that AHG reagent was present and active and washing was adequate. No agglutination → test invalid (repeat).

## Simplified explanation

Check cells are IgG-coated O D-positive cells added to negative antiglobulin tests to prove the AHG reagent worked.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

The antibody screen test for a pregnant woman is tabulated below. The interpretation is that ...

| Cell | Room temperature | 37 °C | AHG |
|---|---|---|---|
| #1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| #2 | +1 | +3 | +4 |
| #3 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
| AUTO | 0 | 0 | 0 |

A. Antibodies are IgG
B. The antibodies are only IgG
C. Autoantibodies are present
D. Multiple antibodies are present
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Antibodies are IgG | **T** | Strong AHG-phase reactivity indicates IgG. |
| B. The antibodies are only IgG | **F** | Room-temperature reactivity suggests an IgM component or a second antibody. |
| C. Autoantibodies are present | **F** | Autocontrol is negative. |
| D. Multiple antibodies are present | **T** | Per the key: reactivity across phases suggests more than one antibody (cold IgM + warm IgG). |

> [!answer]
> **A T, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Phase of reaction suggests antibody class: **IS/room temperature** = IgM (cold, often naturally occurring); **37 °C/AHG** = IgG (warm, clinically significant). A negative **autocontrol** indicates alloantibody. Reactivity at several phases may reflect a mixture of antibodies (e.g. anti-M + anti-D) or an antibody with IgM and IgG components; identification panel needed.

## Simplified explanation

Strong AHG reactions mean IgG; the room-temperature reaction suggests another (IgM) antibody too. The negative autocontrol rules out autoantibodies.
hint: Phase tells class; autocontrol tells auto vs allo.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In vitro methods employed to elute antibodies that had coated red cells in vivo include ...

A. Warm red cells to 64°C
B. Treat red cells with dithiothreitol (DTT) reagent
C. Wash red cells in basic buffer pH 7.5
D. Freezing the red cells
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. Warm red cells to 64°C | **F** | Heat elution uses **56 °C**. |
| B. Treat red cells with dithiothreitol (DTT) reagent | **F** | DTT denatures antigens/IgM; it is not an elution method. |
| C. Wash red cells in basic buffer pH 7.5 | **F** | Elution uses **acid** (glycine-HCl pH ~3) buffer. |
| D. Freezing the red cells | **T** | Freeze-thaw (Lui) elution. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D T**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Elution methods: **heat (56 °C)** (ABO HDFN), **freeze-thaw (Lui)** (ABO), **acid elution** (glycine-HCl/EDTA, pH ~3; most common for IgG), organic solvents (ether, chloroform, xylene), digitonin-acid. Eluates help identify antibodies in DHTR, HDFN and AIHA.

## Simplified explanation

Antibodies can be removed from red cells by freezing (also by heat at 56 °C or acid). DTT and alkaline washing don't elute.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

A negative antibody screening test indicates ...

A. No clinically significant antibodies are present
B. The cross-match will be compatible
C. No adverse reaction could occur in the recipient
D. Addition of Coombs control cells should give negative reaction
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. No clinically significant antibodies are present | **F** | Only that none were detected against antigens on the screening cells (low-frequency antigens or weak antibodies may be missed). |
| B. The cross-match will be compatible | **F** | ABO errors or antibodies to low-incidence antigens can still give incompatibility. |
| C. No adverse reaction could occur in the recipient | **F** | Febrile, allergic, TRALI, TACO and delayed reactions can still occur. |
| D. Addition of Coombs control cells should give negative reaction | **F** | Check cells should **agglutinate** to validate the negative. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C F, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

A negative screen means no detectable unexpected antibody to the antigens represented on the screening cells using that method; it permits electronic/immediate-spin crossmatch in many centres but does not exclude all antibodies or all transfusion reactions. Check cells must give a positive result.

## Simplified explanation

A negative screen doesn't guarantee safety or compatibility, and check cells should then turn positive. All four are false.
hint: Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence.

body:
State whether each option is **true (T)** or **false (F)**.

In considering transfusion therapy ...

A. All patients with [haemoglobin] 9.0 g/dL should receive packed cells
B. Transfusion of whole blood is only indicated when only red cell mass is needed
C. Refractoriness to platelets may result from anti-HLA antibodies
D. One unit of packed red cells should raise the [haemoglobin] by 3 g/dL
answer:
| Option | T/F | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A. All patients with [haemoglobin] 9.0 g/dL should receive packed cells | **F** | Transfusion is guided by clinical state; restrictive thresholds are ~7 g/dL (8 g/dL in cardiac disease). |
| B. Transfusion of whole blood is only indicated when only red cell mass is needed | **F** | Red cell concentrates are used when only red cell mass is needed; whole blood is for combined volume and red cell loss. |
| C. Refractoriness to platelets may result from anti-HLA antibodies | **T** | HLA class I alloimmunisation. |
| D. One unit of packed red cells should raise the [haemoglobin] by 3 g/dL | **F** | About **1 g/dL** in an adult. |

> [!answer]
> **A F, B F, C T, D F**
explanation:
## Advanced explanation

Patient blood management: transfuse according to symptoms and restrictive thresholds, one unit at a time with reassessment; red cell concentrates for anaemia, whole blood (where used) for massive haemorrhage. Platelet refractoriness from HLA antibodies is managed with HLA-matched/crossmatched platelets.

## Simplified explanation

Hb 9 doesn't automatically need blood, whole blood is for volume plus red cells, and one unit raises Hb by about 1 g/dL. Anti-HLA antibodies do cause platelet refractoriness.
